title_patterns: [WELL-KNOWN TICKER] hits a [specific multi-year extreme] after [scheduled event]: is the [specific yield/metric] still covered?
[TICKER] reports [event] tonight — the one number that decides it
[TICKER] could beat [specific expectation]... but [one concrete offsetting constraint]
[TICKER]: the [insider / institutional / buyback] move that didn't make headlines
What [specific unrounded figure] of [revenue / FCF / backlog] actually tells you about [TICKER]
[TICKER] at [price or valuation multiple]: what has to be true for the math to work
[TICKER] vs [peer TICKER] — same sector, two completely different cash flow profiles
[TICKER] after [event]: three numbers that changed and two that didn't
hook_patterns: Open with the single hardest number ('the dividend costs them $X billion a year; operating cash flow was $Y') before naming any opinion.
Name the event and its exact timing, then state the one variable you'll judge it on — no suspense padding.
State the popular take in one sentence, then say which line item you checked to test it.
Start from the chart extreme ('this price was last seen in [year]') and immediately pivot to whether fundamentals match that price.
Lead with the disclosure or filing detail most viewers skipped, then explain what it implies about management's own expectations.
packaging_notes: All three outliers sit in a tight 6-10 minute window — long enough for a full cash-flow or guidance walkthrough, short enough to be one question answered, not a market roundup.
Every title anchors to a single mega-cap-recognizable ticker plus a concrete, checkable catalyst (earnings date, multi-year low, insider filing) rather than 'the market' or macro panic.
Specific unrounded numbers and named percentages in the title outperform vague superlatives; keep the number in the title and resolve it early in the video so the promise is paid off.

A question or tension framing ('is it safe?', 'but there's a problem') works as curiosity without doom — the tension is about a measurable risk, not collapse; keep thumbnails to a clean chart, a filing excerpt, or the number itself.
The 'move you missed' / overlooked-disclosure angle is highly transferable: positions you as the one who reads the 10-Q, which fits a no-hype brand better than prediction titles.
Timing matters more than production: event-adjacent uploads (earnings eve, day-after reaction) captured most of the velocity, so pre-build a template for the two or three companies you cover closest.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns: Shorts: Company + quantified price move + specific catalyst is a promising structure. Three market-close examples pairing percentage moves with merger, spinoff or patent developments recorded 88.8–99.8% average viewed and reported hook-hold values of 1.194–1.357. This is a retention association, not evidence that the title caused distribution.

Shorts: Company or named executive + buy/sell action + dollar amount provides a compact insider-news structure. The purchase example retained 82.7% on average; one CFO-sale example retained 77.7%. Treat this as a modest signal, not a general advantage for insider coverage or large dollar figures.
losing_patterns: Shorts: Avoid relying on an unquantified excitement verb as the main framing. The example combining 'soars' with a disclosure catalyst had 68.0% average viewed, the lowest among these Shorts. One example supports testing more concrete wording, not declaring that wording the cause.

Long videos: Do not assume a large transaction amount plus filing or transaction-count detail is enough to sustain attention. Both long insider-sale videos used that structure but recorded only 38.1–44.9% average viewed and 0.633–0.661 reported hook hold. With only two long videos and no stronger long-form comparator, no winning long-form structure is established.
notes: Market-close Shorts contain the three strongest non-replay APV results, but the 178% price-move example retained less than the 78% example. Bigger headline numbers are not a reliable retention ranking.

The insider-sale Short with 156.1% average viewed and 1.815 hook hold had just 88 views and 24 engaged views. Replay-influenced retention is not proof of broad demand; APV also does not measure swipe-away or feed conversion.

Actual opening scripts were not supplied, so hook wording cannot be evaluated directly. These are tentative title-framing correlations from 10 Shorts and two long videos, not causal findings or a clean format comparison.
